title: Pop-Up Debate Problem: What Do You Do When Students Aren't Yielding the Floor Well e-floor-well/
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Responding to a reader's question about students talking over each other during Pop-Up Debates, Stuart Jr. offers three sequenced interventions for the floor-yielding problem. The first is a post-debate Think-Pair-Share debrief in which students themselves identify the weakness and generate solutions; the second is in-the-moment coaching during the debate itself; the third is a pre-debate mini-lesson that names the causes of the behavior while plainly addressing its costs. Across all three approaches, the governing principle is consistent: make the problem matter-of-fact, impersonal, and solvable rather than a personal indictment of any individual student.
points: A student-led debrief via Think-Pair-Share after a flawed debate surfaces the floor-yielding problem naturally and positions the class as a community identifying and solving a shared challenge.
In-the-moment coaching is more immediate and carries more personal weight, but works best when classroom rapport is already strong enough to receive the feedback as constructive.
Framing yielding failures in terms of their causes — passion, enjoyment of argument — rather than character flaws makes the feedback non-threatening and easier for non-yielding students to accept.
Citing specific costs of not yielding, including fewer ideas heard and peers feeling uncomfortable, gives students practical, student-centered reasons to self-correct.
Making problems 'matter-of-fact, impersonal, and solvable' is the unifying principle across all three interventions, applicable broadly to classroom management beyond the Pop-Up Debate context.
quotes: Dave, what do you do when multiple students stand up at the same time and don't want to yield? I have two class sections where this is becoming a pattern, despite giving them plenty of encouragement and instruction to be courteous with one another and to yield. Do you have any suggestions?

After the next Pop-Up Debate where this happens, save three to five minutes to do a post-debate debrief. This is a simple Think-Pair-Share where you ask students to identify areas where the class did well and areas where the class could do better.

As pairs are sharing out, I like to record what they're saying on a blank slide — all the strengths they mention, all the weaknesses. When they mention a weakness I strongly agree with (e.g., students not yielding well in this case), I underline it and say, 'Yes, this is a weakness of ours. What can we do to solve that?'

Obviously during the Pop-Up Debate where this is happening, this can be one of those ideal moments where I interrupt with some coaching. This approach makes the problem a bit more personal — because you're addressing it right after it's happened — but if there's good rapport in the class, it can be received in a positive and non-threatening manner.

The goal with all of these is to make the problem a matter-of-fact, impersonal reality — it is what it is (problematic), and it is also solvable and improvable. Just about every time, the students creating the problem will respond well to this approach and alter their behavior.
